Suggesting that we have achieved super intelligence is a myth. The present state of GenAI models does not reflect autonomous intellect. If these systems were genuinely super intelligent, Microsoft would not require extensive legal disclaimers stating that the models are unreliable and prone to errors. A system requiring constant human supervision & liability waivers contradicts the concept of super intelligence. Businesses are being asked to assume all operational risk for software that frequently generates incorrect outputs. Also, the essay argues that models should be treated like insider risks within an enterprise. If an organisation must assume that an automated component cannot be trusted and requires continuous quarantine, granting that component administrative authority over company data in the first place makes little practical sense. Agreed in principle,[Satya Nadella](https://www.linkedin.com/in/satyanadella?trk=public_post_comment-text) . But delegating execution to AI creates a practical paradox: human accountability requires meaningful human oversight. If an operator cannot independently assess why a model acted, “oversight” becomes purely symbolic. Audit trails and access controls are a start, but without independently verifiable reasoning and enforceable intervention mechanisms, liability stays with humans while operational control shifts to the machine.

[Satya Nadella](https://www.linkedin.com/in/satyanadella?trk=public_post_comment-text) , the emergency brake has to reach the agents that never received the original human instruction. One agent assigns the work, another hands it off, and a third takes the action. That is where the chain I described in The Provenance Problem gets harder to defend. Withdrawing permission needs to travel through those handoffs, while the evidence of what already happened stays intact.

[Vikram Sharma](https://www.linkedin.com/in/vikram-sharma-a4a31113?trk=public_post_comment_actor-name) 2d


The narrative makes a lot of sense and the recommendation to treat frontier models like privileged insiders is the right one. The part I'd stress-test is reproducing an outcome without relying on the model to attest to it. A lot of agent logging today is the model's own account of what it did, and one recent paper found nearly every harness it tested let the agent delete its own trace when asked. So the record has to come from the harness, somewhere the model can't write. Then someone has to actually replay an outcome from it. In a regulated shop, that's the first thing an auditor will ask for.
